extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and political actors (gentlemen, members of societies, readers interested in the French Revolution and British constitutional questions)
extracted.subtask_description: A political pamphlet / essay offering prescriptive reflections and criticisms of the French Revolution, the conduct of London societies, and proper constitutional, military, and ecclesiastical behaviour. It mixes normative principles, examples, and practical guidance on how revolutions and public bodies should act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing army dangerous to liberty; undisciplined army ruinous to society
rubrics_metrics.description: "An armed disciplined body is, in its essence, dangerous to liberty; undisciplined, it is ruinous to society."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contrasts disciplined standing armies (threat to liberty) with undisciplined forces (dangerous to social order). He argues the necessity of balancing military force with constitutional arrangements and cautions against armies becoming litigants, mutineers, or instruments of sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid divided military command (no partition of armies)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Armies cannot exist under a divided command."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of France's practice of setting up a municipal army under different authority as a 'balance of armies, not of orders'. Burke recommends a single authority and simple oath of fidelity, with the whole army kept under annual inspection to ensure responsibility and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require responsible chain of command and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether crown or any general/colonel/captain is responsible for troops; effective armies require responsibility for conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke emphasizes that conduct of troops must be attributable to commanders and ultimately the crown/government; an absence of responsibility fosters mutiny, treason, and lawlessness (example: nominal commanders dragged with rope around neck).

rubrics_metrics.name: A proper constitutional 'revolution' preserves constituent parts of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: The English Revolution was praised because it 'got rid of the man, and preserved the constituent parts of the state' — no change to fundamental parts of the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues reform should repair and legalize, not overthrow the stable foundations: keep monarchy, church, lords, commons, corporations, franchises, revenue, law and magistracy intact while correcting anomalies; upheaval that destroys social orders risks ruin rather than improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate new liberty by its combination with institutions and social goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Suspend congratulations on 'liberty' until you see how it is combined with government, public force, army discipline, revenue, morality, religion, property, peace, order, and manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke gives an explicit checklist of goods needed alongside liberty for it to be beneficial; he warns that liberty without these is not a lasting or useful blessing and may lead to chaos (analogy: escaped madman or highwayman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political principles must be judged in their circumstances (context matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Circumstances ... give in reality to every political principle its distinguishing color and discriminating effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract doctrines are insufficient; what is beneficial or noxious depends on particular conditions, actors, and history. Burke repeatedly urges judging policies by practical consequences and local conditions rather than metaphysical abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit and church should avoid partisan politics
rubrics_metrics.description: No sound ought to be heard in the church but the healing voice of Christian charity; mixing politics into sermons is improper and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticises Dr. Price's sermon and the use of the pulpit to promulgate political doctrines (e.g., declaring certain kings unlawful), arguing that clergy are generally inexperienced in worldly affairs and that politicizing religion fuels faction and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public resolutions and addresses should show authorship/signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: A vote or resolution 'stands solely on authority' and 'their signatures ought, in my opinion, to have been annexed to their instrument.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that societies issuing authoritative political addresses should reveal who they are and how many sign, so the public can judge the weight of their opinion; anonymous or undifferentiated acts lend a misleading importance to a small body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unauthorized corporate-style correspondence with foreign governments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper and irregular to open formal public correspondence with a foreign government without the express authority of your own government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke objects to societies acting as if they represent national authority when they do not; such acts create ambiguity and may be deceitful or diplomatically improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of political stratagems that use high-sounding names to confer undue authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of giving a club a 'high-sounding name' or public capacity to make its declarations appear like the sense of part of the nation is a policy 'that has very much the complexion of a fraud.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that small groups may seek influence by grand titles and theatrical presentation; the remedy is transparency about membership, motives, and a cautious public attitude toward such proclamations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay political applause until you observe how new power is used
rubrics_metrics.description: When liberty becomes power in bodies, 'considerate people ... will observe the use which is made of power' before declaring praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence requires waiting through the initial effervescence of revolution to judge whether the new powers and actors will act virtuously or dangerously; premature adulation can embolden destructive tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject abstract doctrines that delegitimize one's own constitution without regard to history
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of the doctrine that a king is only lawful if he 'owes his crown to the choice of his people' — applied abstractly, it would make the British king unlawful and is 'dangerous, illegal, and unconstitutional.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke cautions against adopting sweeping theoretical claims about legitimacy that, when taken literally, undercut established constitutional settlement and national security; he suggests such doctrines may be used as future political tools rather than honest principles.
